_note: The Spanish pronunciation rules in the right-hand column of /pronunciation (AusspracheRegeln.astro), in teaching order. `match` is a regular expression tested on the lower-case word without an article: if it matches, the rule is listed under “For this word”. A rule without `match` is general and is never highlighted. `mark` (optional) is the stressed syllable, shown in bold. Castilian Spanish with distinción is the standard; what Latin America does differently is in `es419`, and regional sounds a learner in Spain will hear (seseo, ceceo, a weak final s) are named in the rule text. Rule ids are the old slot ids (content-plan §1.3) plus ll-y and enye. Not yet reviewed by a teacher.

rules.title: The five vowels
rules.text: Spanish has five vowels: a, e, i, o, u. Each one always sounds the same: short and clear, stressed or not. Don't let a vowel glide (no is not “noh-oo”) and don't make it weak: mañana has three full a's.

examples.note: o as in “hot”, with round lips

rules.title: Two vowels together
rules.text: When i or u stands next to a, e or o, the two vowels normally join in one syllable (a diphthong): bien, puerta, aire. Say both, quickly. A written accent on the i or u splits them into two syllables: día is dí-a, país is pa-ís.

rules.title: Word stress: llana and aguda
rules.text: Every word has one strong syllable, and two rules tell you which. A word that ends in a vowel, n or s is stressed on the second-to-last syllable (llana). A word that ends in any other consonant is stressed on the last syllable (aguda). Where a word breaks these rules, it has a written accent.

rules.title: Written accents
rules.text: A written accent shows the strong syllable when the two rules don't. Words stressed three syllables from the end (esdrújulas) always have one: médico, música. An accent can also change the word: hablo (I speak), habló (she spoke); papa (the Pope), papá (dad).

examples.note: ends in a vowel, stressed on the last
ends in l, stressed on the first

rules.title: r and rr
rules.text: A single r between vowels or at the end of a syllable is one quick tap of the tongue tip behind the top teeth: pero, caro, hablar. rr is several quick taps (a trill), and so is r at the start of a word or after n, l, s: perro, carro, rojo. pero (but) and perro (dog) are different words. Neither one is made in the throat.

es419.note: Latin America has seseo: z and c before e, i sound like s, so casa and caza sound the same.

rules.title: c and z: /θ/ (distinción)
rules.text: In most of Spain, z and c before e or i are /θ/, like th in “think”: the tongue tip between the teeth, only air. s stays /s/, so casa (house) and caza (hunting) are different words. c before a, o, u is /k/. You will also hear seseo (s for /θ/) in the Canaries and much of Andalusia, and ceceo (/θ/ for s too) in parts of Andalusia. Both are normal there, not mistakes.

es419.note: Much of Latin America also weakens a final s, especially the Caribbean, Argentina and Chile.

rules.title: s never buzzes
rules.text: Spanish s is the s in “sun”, also between vowels. Don't make it a buzzing z: casa, mesa, museo. In southern Spain and the Canaries a final s often becomes a breath or disappears: los amigos can sound like “loh amigoh”. You will hear this, but you don't have to copy it.

es419.note: In the Caribbean, Central America and Colombia this sound is softer, close to the h in “house”.

rules.title: j, and g before e or i: /x/
rules.text: j, and g before e or i, are /x/: a rasp at the back of the mouth, like ch in Scottish “loch”. In Spain it is strong and clearly audible. It is not the j in “jam”. g before a, o, u is the g in “go”: gato, amigo.

es419.note: In Argentina and Uruguay ll and y often sound like sh or the s in “measure”.

rules.title: ll and y (yeísmo)
rules.text: In most of Spain ll and y are one sound (yeísmo): like y in “yes”, a little stronger. Some older speakers in rural areas still keep ll apart. It is never an l: calle, not “cale”. On its own or at the end of a word, y is a vowel, like i: y (and), hoy, muy.

rules.title: ñ
rules.text: ñ is one sound, like ny in “canyon” or gn in French and Italian. Press the middle of your tongue against the roof of your mouth. It is a letter of its own, and it changes the word: pena (sorrow), peña (rock; a group of friends).

rules.title: b and v: one sound
rules.text: b and v sound exactly the same. At the start of a phrase and after m or n, close both lips: vino, bien, un vaso. Between vowels your lips almost touch, and the sound is soft: abuela, nuevo. Your top teeth never touch your lip.

rules.title: Hard and soft d
rules.text: At the start of a phrase and after n or l, d is hard, with the tongue against the top teeth: dos, donde. Everywhere else it is soft /ð/, like th in “this”: nada, cansado. At the end of a word it is very weak: Madrid, usted. In relaxed speech in Spain, -ado often sounds like “-ao”: cansao.

rules.title: h is silent
rules.text: You never say the letter h. Start straight on the next vowel: hola sounds just like ola (wave). h only has a sound together with c, as ch.

rules.title: ch
rules.text: ch is one sound, as in “church”: ocho, noche, leche. It is not sh, and it is not k.

rules.title: qu, gu and gü
rules.text: In que and qui the u is silent and the sound is /k/: queso, quiero. In gue and gui the u is silent too and the g is the one in “go”: guerra, guitarra. Only with two dots (ü) do you say the u: vergüenza, pingüino.

rules.title: Linking words
rules.text: Spanish flows from word to word with no stop. A last vowel and a first vowel join in one syllable (sinalefa): mi amigo. A last consonant moves on to the next vowel: los otros sounds like “lo-so-tros”.
